Now I have a clear picture of your setup. You're using Drizzle ORM with Turso (SQLite) and better-auth. Let me help you design a clean and practical schema for your portfolio CMS.

## My Recommendations

### 1. Technologies vs Soft-skills/Practices

**My recommendation: One unified `skills` table with a `type` column.**

Why?
- Simpler schema, fewer junction tables
- Both have the same basic structure (name, maybe icon/url)
- Easy to filter by type
- Flexible to add more types later (tools, methodologies, languages, frameworks...)

```typescript
export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  name: text("name").notNull(),
  type: text("type", { enum: ["technology", "practice"] }).notNull(),
  icon: text("icon"), // URL or icon name (e.g., "react", "typescript")
  url: text("url"),   // Optional link to official site
});
```

Then you'll need junction tables for the many-to-many relationships:
- `project_skills`
- `experience_skills`

---

### 2. Employment Status

**My recommendation: A single-row `site_settings` table that you UPDATE.**

Why?
- Simpler queries (`SELECT * FROM site_settings LIMIT 1`)
- No accumulating rows
- Extensible for future settings (maintenance mode, theme, etc.)
- If you need history, you can always add an audit log later

```typescript
export const siteSettings = sqliteTable("site_settings", {
  id: integer("id").primaryKey().default(1), // Always 1
  isEmployed: integer("is_employed", { mode: "boolean" }).default(false).notNull(),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
});
```

---

### 3. Additional Tables to Consider

| Table | Purpose | Fields |
|-------|---------|--------|
| `social_links` | GitHub, LinkedIn, Twitter, etc. | id, name, url, icon, order |
| `education` | Degrees, bootcamps | id, institution, degree, field, start_date, end_date |
| `certifications` | Professional certs | id, name, issuer, date, url, badge_url |

For a portfolio, I'd say **`social_links` is almost essential**. Education and certifications depend on your needs.

### 4. Suggested Complete Schema

Here's how I'd structure your portfolio schema:

```typescript
// db/schema/portfolio.ts
import { relations, sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { sqliteTable, text, integer, index, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

// ============ PROJECTS ============
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
  description: text("description").notNull(),
  url: text("url"),
  image: text("image"),        // Project thumbnail/screenshot
  featured: integer("featured", { mode: "boolean" }).default(false),
  order: integer("order").default(0),  // For manual sorting
  createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .notNull(),
});

// ============ EXPERIENCES ============
export const experiences = sqliteTable("experiences", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  role: text("role").notNull(),
  company: text("company").notNull(),
  companyUrl: text("company_url"),
  companyLogo: text("company_logo"),
  description: text("description").notNull(),
  startDate: integer("start_date", { mode: "timestamp_ms" }).notNull(),
  endDate: integer("end_date", { mode: "timestamp_ms" }), // NULL = current job
  order: integer("order").default(0),
});

// ============ SKILLS (Technologies + Practices) ============
export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  name: text("name").notNull(),
  type: text("type").notNull(), // "technology" | "practice"
  icon: text("icon"),
  url: text("url"),
});

// ============ JUNCTION TABLES ============
export const projectSkills = sqliteTable("project_skills", {
  projectId: text("project_id").notNull().references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  skillId: text("skill_id").notNull().references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (table) => [
  primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] }),
]);

export const experienceSkills = sqliteTable("experience_skills", {
  experienceId: text("experience_id").notNull().references(() => experiences.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  skillId: text("skill_id").notNull().references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (table) => [
  primaryKey({ columns: [table.experienceId, table.skillId] }),
]);

// ============ SOCIAL LINKS ============
export const socialLinks = sqliteTable("social_links", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  name: text("name").notNull(),       // "GitHub", "LinkedIn"
  url: text("url").notNull(),
  icon: text("icon"),                 // "github", "linkedin"
  order: integer("order").default(0),
});

// ============ SITE SETTINGS ============
export const siteSettings = sqliteTable("site_settings", {
  id: integer("id").primaryKey().default(1),
  isEmployed: integer("is_employed", { mode: "boolean" }).default(false).notNull(),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
});

// ============ RELATIONS ============
export const projectRelations = relations(projects, ({ many }) => ({
  skills: many(projectSkills),
}));

export const experienceRelations = relations(experiences, ({ many }) => ({
  skills: many(experienceSkills),
}));

export const skillRelations = relations(skills, ({ many }) => ({
  projects: many(projectSkills),
  experiences: many(experienceSkills),
}));

export const projectSkillRelations = relations(projectSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  project: one(projects, {
    fields: [projectSkills.projectId],
    references: [projects.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [projectSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));

export const experienceSkillRelations = relations(experienceSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  experience: one(experiences, {
    fields: [experienceSkills.experienceId],
    references: [experiences.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [experienceSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));
```

Great question! Let me explain what an audit log is and how you can use it to build a history view in your CMS.

## What is an Audit Log?

An **audit log** (or **history table**) is a separate table that records every change made to your data. Instead of only keeping the current state, you also **insert a new row** into the history table each time something changes.

This gives you:
- **When** the change happened
- **What** the previous/new value was
- **Who** made the change (optional, useful for multi-user systems)

---

## How It Works for Employment Status

You'd have **two tables**:

| Table | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `site_settings` | Current state (single row, always UPDATE) |
| `employment_history` | Audit log (INSERT new row on every change) |

```typescript
// Current state - for quick queries
export const siteSettings = sqliteTable("site_settings", {
  id: integer("id").primaryKey().default(1),
  isEmployed: integer("is_employed", { mode: "boolean" }).default(false).notNull(),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
});

// Audit log - for history visualization
export const employmentHistory = sqliteTable("employment_history", {
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  isEmployed: integer("is_employed", { mode: "boolean" }).notNull(),
  changedAt: integer("changed_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .notNull(),
  // Optional: track who made the change
  changedBy: text("changed_by").references(() => users.id),
});
```

---

## How to Use It

When you toggle employment status in your CMS, you do **two operations**:

```typescript
// In your API route or server action
async function toggleEmploymentStatus(newStatus: boolean, userId: string) {
  // 1. Update current state
  await db.update(siteSettings)
    .set({ isEmployed: newStatus })
    .where(eq(siteSettings.id, 1));

  // 2. Insert into history log
  await db.insert(employmentHistory).values({
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    isEmployed: newStatus,
    changedBy: userId,
  });
}
```

---

## Querying for Your Dashboard

```typescript
// Get current status (fast, single row)
const current = await db.select().from(siteSettings).limit(1);

// Get full history for visualization (newest first)
const history = await db
  .select()
  .from(employmentHistory)
  .orderBy(desc(employmentHistory.changedAt));
```

---

## Visual Example in Your CMS

With this data, you could build a timeline like:

| Date | Status | Changed By |
|------|--------|------------|
| Nov 28, 2025 - 10:30 AM | 🟢 Employed | You |
| Oct 15, 2025 - 3:45 PM | 🔴 Unemployed | You |
| Jun 1, 2025 - 9:00 AM | 🟢 Employed | You |
| Jan 10, 2025 - 2:15 PM | 🔴 Unemployed | You |

You could even calculate durations between changes to show things like:
- "Employed for 1 month, 13 days"
- "Job search lasted 4 months, 14 days"

---

## Summary

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| **Single row only** | Simple, fast queries | No history |
| **Append-only (no current state)** | Full history | Slower to get current state |
| **Both tables (recommended)** | Fast current queries + full history | Slightly more complex writes |

The **two-table approach** gives you the best of both worlds: fast reads for the public site and complete history for your CMS dashboard.

## 1. Junction Tables in Drizzle (SQLite)

Junction tables need a **composite primary key** using both foreign keys:

```typescript
import { sqliteTable, text, integer, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

// Junction: Projects ↔ Skills
export const projectSkills = sqliteTable("project_skills", {
  projectId: integer("project_id")
    .notNull()
    .references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  skillId: integer("skill_id")
    .notNull()
    .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (table) => [
  primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] }),
]);

// Junction: Experiences ↔ Skills
export const experienceSkills = sqliteTable("experience_skills", {
  experienceId: integer("experience_id")
    .notNull()
    .references(() => experiences.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  skillId: integer("skill_id")
    .notNull()
    .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (table) => [
  primaryKey({ columns: [table.experienceId, table.skillId] }),
]);
```

**Key points:**
- Import `primaryKey` from `drizzle-orm/sqlite-core`
- The third argument to `sqliteTable` is a function that returns an array of indexes/constraints
- `onDelete: "cascade"` means: if you delete a project, all its `project_skills` rows are deleted too

---

## 2. Order Field (Manual Sorting)

The `order` field should **NOT** be auto-increment in the database. It's just a regular integer that your **application code** manages:

```typescript
// In your table definition
order: integer("order").notNull().default(0),
```

**Why not auto-increment?**
- Auto-increment is for IDs (unique, never changes)
- Order needs to be **updatable** for drag-and-drop reordering

**How to handle it in your application code:**

```typescript
// When INSERTING a new project, get max order + 1
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";

async function createProject(data: NewProject) {
  // Get current max order
  const result = await db
    .select({ maxOrder: sql<number>`COALESCE(MAX(${projects.order}), 0)` })
    .from(projects);
  
  const newOrder = result[0].maxOrder + 1;

  await db.insert(projects).values({
    ...data,
    order: newOrder,
  });
}

// When REORDERING (drag-and-drop), just update the order values
async function reorderProjects(orderedIds: number[]) {
  // orderedIds = [3, 1, 5, 2] means project 3 is first, project 1 is second, etc.
  for (let i = 0; i < orderedIds.length; i++) {
    await db
      .update(projects)
      .set({ order: i })
      .where(eq(projects.id, orderedIds[i]));
  }
}
```

---

## 3. Enums in Drizzle (SQLite)

SQLite doesn't have native ENUMs like PostgreSQL. Drizzle handles this with the `text` type and an `enum` option for **TypeScript type safety**:

```typescript
// Option A: Inline enum
status: text("status", { enum: ["active", "archived", "in-progress"] })
  .notNull()
  .default("active"),

// Option B: Separate const (recommended - reusable)
export const projectStatuses = ["active", "archived", "in-progress"] as const;
export type ProjectStatus = (typeof projectStatuses)[number];

// Then in the table:
status: text("status", { enum: projectStatuses }).notNull().default("active"),
```

**For your tables:**

```typescript
// Define your enums at the top of the file
export const projectStatuses = ["active", "archived", "in-progress"] as const;
export const skillTypes = ["technology", "practice"] as const;

// Use them in tables
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  // ...
  status: text("status", { enum: projectStatuses }).notNull().default("active"),
});

export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  // ...
  type: text("type", { enum: skillTypes }).notNull(),
});
```

```typescript
import { relations } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { integer, pgTable, primaryKey, serial, text } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

export const users = pgTable('users', {
  id: serial('id').primaryKey(),
  name: text('name'),
});

export const usersRelations = relations(users, ({ many }) => ({
  usersToGroups: many(usersToGroups),
}));

export const groups = pgTable('groups', {
  id: serial('id').primaryKey(),
  name: text('name'),
});

export const groupsRelations = relations(groups, ({ many }) => ({
  usersToGroups: many(usersToGroups),
}));

  'users_to_groups',
  {
    userId: integer('user_id')
      .notNull()
      .references(() => users.id),
    groupId: integer('group_id')
      .notNull()
      .references(() => groups.id),
  },
  (t) => [
    primaryKey({ columns: [t.userId, t.groupId] })
  ],
);

export const usersToGroupsRelations = relations(usersToGroups, ({ one }) => ({
  group: one(groups, {
    fields: [usersToGroups.groupId],
    references: [groups.id],
  }),
  user: one(users, {
    fields: [usersToGroups.userId],
    references: [users.id],
  }),
}));
```

You're absolutely right! The `relations` function is needed to use Drizzle's **relational query API** (the `db.query.*.findMany({ with: {...} })` syntax). Let me explain the complete picture.

---

## Two Separate Concepts

| Concept | Purpose | Required for |
|---------|---------|--------------|
| **Foreign keys** (`.references()`) | Database-level constraints | Data integrity |
| **Relations** (`relations()`) | Application-level definitions | Relational queries (`with: {}`) |

They work **independently** but are usually used **together**.

---

## Complete Many-to-Many Setup

According to the [Drizzle Relations docs](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations#many-to-many), for many-to-many you need:

1. **Junction table** with foreign keys + composite primary key
2. **Relations on parent tables** → pointing to the junction table (`many`)
3. **Relations on junction table** → pointing back to both parents (`one`)

---

## For Your Schema (Projects ↔ Skills, Experiences ↔ Skills)

```typescript
import { relations } from "drizzle-orm";
import { sqliteTable, text, integer, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

// ============ TABLES ============

export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  // ... your other fields
});

export const experiences = sqliteTable("experiences", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  // ... your other fields
});

export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  // ... your other fields
});

// ============ JUNCTION TABLES ============

export const projectSkills = sqliteTable(
  "project_skills",
  {
    projectId: integer("project_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    skillId: integer("skill_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  },
  (table) => [
    primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] }),
  ]
);

export const experienceSkills = sqliteTable(
  "experience_skills",
  {
    experienceId: integer("experience_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => experiences.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    skillId: integer("skill_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  },
  (table) => [
    primaryKey({ columns: [table.experienceId, table.skillId] }),
  ]
);

// ============ RELATIONS ============

// Projects relations
export const projectsRelations = relations(projects, ({ many }) => ({
  projectSkills: many(projectSkills),
}));

// Experiences relations
export const experiencesRelations = relations(experiences, ({ many }) => ({
  experienceSkills: many(experienceSkills),
}));

// Skills relations (connected to both junction tables)
export const skillsRelations = relations(skills, ({ many }) => ({
  projectSkills: many(projectSkills),
  experienceSkills: many(experienceSkills),
}));

// Junction table relations (connect back to both parent tables)
export const projectSkillsRelations = relations(projectSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  project: one(projects, {
    fields: [projectSkills.projectId],
    references: [projects.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [projectSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));

export const experienceSkillsRelations = relations(experienceSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  experience: one(experiences, {
    fields: [experienceSkills.experienceId],
    references: [experiences.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [experienceSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));
```

---

## What This Enables

With these relations defined, you can use Drizzle's relational query API:

```typescript
// Get all projects with their skills
const projectsWithSkills = await db.query.projects.findMany({
  with: {
    projectSkills: {
      with: {
        skill: true,
      },
    },
  },
});

// Result structure:
// {
//   id: 1,
//   title: "My Portfolio",
//   projectSkills: [
//     { projectId: 1, skillId: 1, skill: { id: 1, name: "React", type: "technology" } },
//     { projectId: 1, skillId: 2, skill: { id: 2, name: "TypeScript", type: "technology" } },
//   ]
// }
```

---

## Summary

| Part | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `.references()` on junction table | Creates foreign key constraint in DB |
| `primaryKey({ columns: [...] })` | Creates composite primary key |
| `relations()` on parent tables | `many(junctionTable)` - enables relational queries |
| `relations()` on junction table | `one(parentA)` + `one(parentB)` - connects back to parents |

The [Drizzle docs](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations#many-to-many) have this exact pattern in their users ↔ groups example!

## Part 1: The Problem - Many-to-Many Relationships

Imagine you have:
- **Projects**: "My Portfolio", "E-commerce App", "Blog"
- **Skills**: "React", "TypeScript", "Node.js"

The relationship is **many-to-many**:
- One project can have **many skills** (Portfolio uses React, TypeScript, Node.js)
- One skill can belong to **many projects** (React is used in Portfolio AND E-commerce)

**You can't store this directly in either table.** Why?

```
❌ If you add a skill_id column to projects:
   projects: { id: 1, title: "Portfolio", skill_id: ??? }
   → But Portfolio has 3 skills! Where do you put them?

❌ If you add a project_id column to skills:
   skills: { id: 1, name: "React", project_id: ??? }
   → But React is in 2 projects! Where do you put them?
```

---

## Part 2: The Solution - Junction Table

A **junction table** (also called "join table" or "pivot table") stores the **relationships** between two tables:

```
projects table:          skills table:           project_skills table:
┌────┬─────────────┐     ┌────┬────────────┐     ┌────────────┬──────────┐
│ id │ title       │     │ id │ name       │     │ project_id │ skill_id │
├────┼─────────────┤     ├────┼────────────┤     ├────────────┼──────────┤
│ 1  │ Portfolio   │     │ 1  │ React      │     │ 1          │ 1        │  ← Portfolio has React
│ 2  │ E-commerce  │     │ 2  │ TypeScript │     │ 1          │ 2        │  ← Portfolio has TypeScript
│ 3  │ Blog        │     │ 3  │ Node.js    │     │ 1          │ 3        │  ← Portfolio has Node.js
└────┴─────────────┘     └────┴────────────┘     │ 2          │ 1        │  ← E-commerce has React
                                                 │ 2          │ 2        │  ← E-commerce has TypeScript
                                                 │ 3          │ 3        │  ← Blog has Node.js
                                                 └────────────┴──────────┘
```

Now you can answer questions like:
- "What skills does Portfolio have?" → Look for rows where `project_id = 1`
- "Which projects use React?" → Look for rows where `skill_id = 1`

---

## Part 3: Creating the Junction Table in Drizzle

```typescript
import { sqliteTable, integer, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

export const projectSkills = sqliteTable(
  "project_skills",  // ← Table name
  {
    // Column 1: Foreign key to projects
    projectId: integer("project_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    
    // Column 2: Foreign key to skills
    skillId: integer("skill_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  },
  // Third argument: constraints/indexes
  (table) => [
    primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] }),
  ]
);
```

Let me explain each part:

### 3.1 The Foreign Key Columns

```typescript
projectId: integer("project_id")
  .notNull()                                              // ← Must have a value
  .references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }) // ← Points to projects.id
```

- `.references(() => projects.id)` creates a **foreign key constraint**
- This tells the database: "This value MUST exist in the `projects.id` column"
- If you try to insert `projectId: 999` and there's no project with `id: 999`, the database will **reject** it

### 3.2 The `onDelete: "cascade"` Option

```typescript
.references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" })
```

This means: "If the referenced project is deleted, automatically delete this row too"

Example:
```
Before deleting project 1:
project_skills: [
  { project_id: 1, skill_id: 1 },  ← Will be auto-deleted
  { project_id: 1, skill_id: 2 },  ← Will be auto-deleted
  { project_id: 2, skill_id: 1 },  ← Will stay
]

After deleting project 1:
project_skills: [
  { project_id: 2, skill_id: 1 },  ← Still here
]
```

Without cascade, deleting project 1 would **fail** because there are rows referencing it.

### 3.3 The Composite Primary Key

```typescript
(table) => [
  primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] }),
]
```

This creates a **composite primary key** using BOTH columns together.

Why? To prevent duplicates:
```
✅ (project_id: 1, skill_id: 1)  ← OK, first time
✅ (project_id: 1, skill_id: 2)  ← OK, different skill
✅ (project_id: 2, skill_id: 1)  ← OK, different project
❌ (project_id: 1, skill_id: 1)  ← ERROR! Duplicate - Portfolio already has React
```

The combination of `(project_id, skill_id)` must be unique.

---

## Part 4: What is `relations()` and Why Do We Need It?

Now here's the important distinction:

| Concept | Level | Purpose |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `.references()` | **Database** | Enforces data integrity (constraints) |
| `relations()` | **Application** | Enables Drizzle's relational query API |

**They are independent!** You can have one without the other.

### Without `relations()`:

You can still query data, but you have to do **manual joins**:

```typescript
// Manual join - works, but verbose
const result = await db
  .select()
  .from(projects)
  .leftJoin(projectSkills, eq(projectSkills.projectId, projects.id))
  .leftJoin(skills, eq(skills.id, projectSkills.skillId));

// Result is flat, you have to manually group it
```

### With `relations()`:

You can use the **relational query API** with `with: {}`:

```typescript
// Relational query - clean and easy
const result = await db.query.projects.findMany({
  with: {
    projectSkills: {
      with: {
        skill: true,
      },
    },
  },
});

// Result is already nested!
// { id: 1, title: "Portfolio", projectSkills: [{ skill: { name: "React" } }, ...] }
```

---

## Part 5: How `relations()` Works

The `relations()` function tells Drizzle **how tables are connected** at the application level.

### 5.1 Relations on Parent Tables

```typescript
export const projectsRelations = relations(projects, ({ many }) => ({
  projectSkills: many(projectSkills),
}));
```

Let's break this down:

```typescript
relations(
  projects,           // ← Which table are we defining relations for?
  ({ many }) => ({    // ← Destructure the helpers (many, one)
    projectSkills: many(projectSkills),  // ← "projects has MANY projectSkills rows"
  })
);
```

- `many(projectSkills)` means: "One project can have many rows in the projectSkills table"
- The property name `projectSkills` becomes the key you use in `with: { projectSkills: true }`

### 5.2 Relations on Junction Table

```typescript
export const projectSkillsRelations = relations(projectSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  project: one(projects, {
    fields: [projectSkills.projectId],
    references: [projects.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [projectSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));
```

Let's break this down:

```typescript
project: one(projects, {
  fields: [projectSkills.projectId],  // ← "projectSkills.projectId..."
  references: [projects.id],          // ← "...points to projects.id"
}),
```

- `one(projects, {...})` means: "Each projectSkills row belongs to ONE project"
- `fields` = the column in THIS table (projectSkills)
- `references` = the column in the OTHER table (projects)

This tells Drizzle: "To find the project for a projectSkills row, match `projectSkills.projectId` with `projects.id`"

---

## Part 6: The Complete Picture

Here's how all the pieces work together:

```typescript
// ============ 1. TABLES (with foreign keys for DB integrity) ============

export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer("id").primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
});

export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  id: integer("id").primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text("name").notNull(),
});

export const projectSkills = sqliteTable(
  "project_skills",
  {
    projectId: integer("project_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => projects.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    skillId: integer("skill_id")
      .notNull()
      .references(() => skills.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  },
  (table) => [primaryKey({ columns: [table.projectId, table.skillId] })]
);

// ============ 2. RELATIONS (for Drizzle relational queries) ============

// "A project has many projectSkills"
export const projectsRelations = relations(projects, ({ many }) => ({
  projectSkills: many(projectSkills),
}));

// "A skill has many projectSkills"
export const skillsRelations = relations(skills, ({ many }) => ({
  projectSkills: many(projectSkills),
}));

// "A projectSkills row belongs to one project AND one skill"
export const projectSkillsRelations = relations(projectSkills, ({ one }) => ({
  project: one(projects, {
    fields: [projectSkills.projectId],
    references: [projects.id],
  }),
  skill: one(skills, {
    fields: [projectSkills.skillId],
    references: [skills.id],
  }),
}));
```

---

## Part 7: Using It in Queries

### Insert a relationship:

```typescript
// Add React skill to Portfolio project
await db.insert(projectSkills).values({
  projectId: 1,  // Portfolio
  skillId: 1,    // React
});
```

### Query with relations:

```typescript
// Get Portfolio with all its skills
const portfolio = await db.query.projects.findFirst({
  where: eq(projects.id, 1),
  with: {
    projectSkills: {
      with: {
        skill: true,  // Include the actual skill data
      },
    },
  },
});

// Result:
// {
//   id: 1,
//   title: "Portfolio",
//   projectSkills: [
//     { 
//       projectId: 1, 
//       skillId: 1, 
//       skill: { id: 1, name: "React", type: "technology" } 
//     },
//     { 
//       projectId: 1, 
//       skillId: 2, 
//       skill: { id: 2, name: "TypeScript", type: "technology" } 
//     },
//   ]
// }
```

---

## Summary

| Component | What it does | Required for |
|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| Junction table | Stores relationships (project_id, skill_id pairs) | Many-to-many data |
| `.references()` | Database constraint - ensures valid IDs | Data integrity |
| `onDelete: "cascade"` | Auto-delete junction rows when parent is deleted | Clean deletion |
| `primaryKey({ columns: [...] })` | Prevents duplicate relationships | Unique pairs |
| `relations()` with `many()` | "This table has many rows in that table" | Relational queries |
| `relations()` with `one()` | "Each row in this table points to one row in that table" | Relational queries |

Does this make the concepts clearer? Let me know if you want me to explain any part in more detail!

---

Great question! You can create a **reusable timestamps object** and spread it into each table. Here's how:

---

## The Solution: Spread Operator

Create a `timestamps` object once, then use `...timestamps` in every table:

```typescript
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { integer } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

// ============ REUSABLE TIMESTAMPS ============
export const timestamps = {
  createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .notNull(),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
};
```

---

## How to Use It

```typescript
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
  description: text("description").notNull(),
  // ... other fields
  ...timestamps,  // ← Spread here!
});

export const experiences = sqliteTable("experiences", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  role: text("role").notNull(),
  // ... other fields
  ...timestamps,  // ← Same here!
});

export const skills = sqliteTable("skills", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text("name").notNull(),
  // ... other fields
  ...timestamps,  // ← And here!
});
```

---

## How It Works

| Field | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `created_at` | Auto-set to current time on **INSERT** (via SQL default) |
| `updated_at` | Auto-set on **INSERT**, auto-updated on every **UPDATE** (via `$onUpdate`) |

### The SQL Expression

```typescript
.default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
```

This is SQLite's way of getting the current timestamp in milliseconds:
- `unixepoch('subsecond')` → Current Unix time with subsecond precision
- `* 1000` → Convert to milliseconds
- `cast(... as integer)` → Store as integer

### The `$onUpdate` Hook

```typescript
.$onUpdate(() => new Date())
```

This tells Drizzle: "Every time this row is updated, set `updated_at` to the current time."

---

## Complete Example

Here's how your imports should look at the top of your file:

```typescript
import { relations, sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { sqliteTable, text, integer, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";

// ============ REUSABLE TIMESTAMPS ============
export const timestamps = {
  createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .notNull(),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
};

// ============ TABLES ============
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
  // ... other fields
  ...timestamps,
});

// ... rest of your tables
```

---

## Which Tables Need Timestamps?

Based on your TODOs:

| Table | Needs `...timestamps`? |
|-------|------------------------|
| `projects` | ✅ Yes |
| `experiences` | ✅ Yes |
| `skills` | ✅ Yes |
| `projectSkills` | ✅ Yes (optional, but useful) |
| `experienceSkills` | ✅ Yes (optional, but useful) |
| `siteSettings` | ❌ Only needs `updatedAt` |
| `employmentHistory` | ❌ Only needs `changedAt` (which is like `createdAt`) |
| `socialLinks` | ✅ Yes |

---

## Bonus: For Tables That Only Need One Timestamp

For `siteSettings` (only `updated_at`) and `employmentHistory` (only `changed_at`), you can create separate helpers:

```typescript
// Only updated_at
export const updatedAtTimestamp = {
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date())
    .notNull(),
};

// Only changed_at (same as created_at, but different name)
export const changedAtTimestamp = {
  changedAt: integer("changed_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
    .default(sql`(cast(unixepoch('subsecond') * 1000 as integer))`)
    .notNull(),
};
```

Then use them:

```typescript
export const siteSettings = sqliteTable("site_settings", {
  // ... fields
  ...updatedAtTimestamp,
});

export const employmentHistory = sqliteTable("employment_history", {
  // ... fields
  ...changedAtTimestamp,
});
```

---

## In the Database (Raw SQLite)

The value stored is a **big integer** representing milliseconds since January 1, 1970 (Unix epoch):

```
created_at: 1732984523456
```

That number `1732984523456` means:
- **1,732,984,523,456 milliseconds** since Jan 1, 1970
- Which equals: **Saturday, November 30, 2024, 3:15:23.456 PM UTC**

---

## Visual Example

If you query your database directly (e.g., with a SQLite viewer):

```sql
SELECT * FROM projects;
```

| id | title | description | created_at | updated_at |
|----|-------|-------------|------------|------------|
| 1 | Portfolio | My personal site | 1732984523456 | 1732984523456 |
| 2 | E-commerce | Online store | 1732980000000 | 1732984000000 |

Just raw numbers - that's how SQLite stores it.

---

## In Your TypeScript Code (Drizzle)

When you query with Drizzle, the `{ mode: "timestamp_ms" }` option **automatically converts** it to a JavaScript `Date` object:

```typescript
const project = await db.query.projects.findFirst();

console.log(project.createdAt);
// Output: Date object → 2024-11-30T15:15:23.456Z

console.log(project.createdAt.toLocaleDateString());
// Output: "11/30/2024"

console.log(project.createdAt.getTime());
// Output: 1732984523456 (the raw number)
```

---

## The Conversion Flow

```
INSERT → JavaScript Date → Drizzle converts → Integer stored in DB
                            (1732984523456)

SELECT → Integer from DB → Drizzle converts → JavaScript Date
         (1732984523456)                      (Date object)
```

---

## Why Use `timestamp_ms` Instead of `timestamp`?

| Mode | Stores | Precision |
|------|--------|-----------|
| `timestamp` | Seconds (1732984523) | 1 second |
| `timestamp_ms` | Milliseconds (1732984523456) | 1 millisecond |

`timestamp_ms` is more precise - useful if you need to track exact order of events that happen within the same second.

---

## Summary

| Layer | What you see |
|-------|--------------|
| **SQLite Database** | `1732984523456` (integer) |
| **TypeScript/Drizzle** | `Date` object (e.g., `2024-11-30T15:15:23.456Z`) |
| **Your UI** | Whatever format you want (e.g., "Nov 30, 2024") |

## Why Store It This Way?

| Approach | Stored as | Pros | Cons |
|----------|-----------|------|------|
| **Unix timestamp** (your approach) | `1732984523456` | Fast to compare, sort, calculate differences | Not human-readable in DB |
| Separate columns | year, month, day, hour... | Human-readable | 6+ columns, harder to query |
| ISO string | `"2024-11-30T15:15:23.456Z"` | Human-readable | Slower to compare, uses more storage |

**Unix timestamps are the standard** for databases - they're efficient and contain all the information you need.

Good question! Here's the difference between the two modes:

---

## `timestamp` vs `timestamp_ms`

| Mode | Stores | Precision | Example Value |
|------|--------|-----------|---------------|
| `timestamp` | **Seconds** since Jan 1, 1970 | 1 second | `1732984523` |
| `timestamp_ms` | **Milliseconds** since Jan 1, 1970 | 1 millisecond | `1732984523456` |

---

## Visual Comparison

Both represent the same moment: **November 30, 2024, 3:15:23.456 PM**

```
timestamp mode:
┌─────────────────────────┐
│  1732984523             │  ← 10 digits (seconds)
│  2024-11-30T15:15:23Z   │  ← No milliseconds!
└─────────────────────────┘

timestamp_ms mode:
┌─────────────────────────┐
│  1732984523456          │  ← 13 digits (milliseconds)
│  2024-11-30T15:15:23.456Z│  ← Has milliseconds!
└─────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Code Example

```typescript
// Using timestamp (seconds)
createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp" })

// Using timestamp_ms (milliseconds)  
createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })
```

**In your TypeScript code**, both return a JavaScript `Date` object:

```typescript

// Both modes give you a Date object
console.log(project.createdAt); // Date object
```

**But the precision differs:**

```typescript
// With timestamp (seconds) - milliseconds are lost
date.getMilliseconds(); // Always 0

// With timestamp_ms (milliseconds) - full precision
date.getMilliseconds(); // 456 (actual value)
```

---

## When Does Precision Matter?

| Scenario | Does it matter? |
|----------|-----------------|
| "When was this blog post created?" | ❌ No - second precision is fine |
| "Sort events that happened in the same second" | ✅ Yes - need milliseconds |
| "Track exact order of rapid user actions" | ✅ Yes - need milliseconds |
| "Display 'Created on Nov 30, 2024'" | ❌ No - second precision is fine |

---

## My Recommendation

**Use `timestamp_ms`** (what you have now) - it's:
- More precise (you never lose data)
- Standard in modern JavaScript (Date uses milliseconds internally)
- Same storage cost in SQLite (both are just integers)

```typescript
// ✅ Recommended
integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp_ms" })

// ⚠️ Less precise (but works fine for most cases)
integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp" })
```

---

## Summary

| Mode | Stored Value | JavaScript Output |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| `timestamp` | `1732984523` (seconds) | `Date` with 0 milliseconds |
| `timestamp_ms` | `1732984523456` (milliseconds) | `Date` with full precision |

Great question! Yes, Drizzle has a **casing** feature that automatically converts camelCase property names to snake_case column names. This way you don't have to manually specify column names!

---

## The Problem You Have Now

Currently you're doing this manually:

```typescript
// You have to specify "repo_url" manually
repoUrl: text("repo_url"),
companyUrl: text("company_url"),
startDate: integer("start_date", { mode: 'timestamp_ms' }),
```

---

## The Solution: `casing` Option

Drizzle supports automatic casing conversion. You configure it in **two places**:

### 1. In your `drizzle.config.ts`

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from "drizzle-kit";

export default defineConfig({
  dialect: "sqlite",
  schema: "./db/schema/*",
  out: "./db/migrations",
  casing: "snake_case",  // ← Add this!
  // ... rest of your config
});
```

### 2. In your database client (`db/index.ts`)

```typescript
import { createClient } from "@libsql/client";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/libsql";

const client = createClient({
  url: process.env.TURSO_DATABASE_URL!,
  authToken: process.env.TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN!,
});

export const db = drizzle(client, {
  casing: "snake_case",  // ← Add this!
});
```

---

## How Your Schema Would Look

**Before (manual column names):**

```typescript
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
  repoUrl: text("repo_url"),  // ← Manual
  companyUrl: text("company_url"),  // ← Manual
  startDate: integer("start_date", { mode: 'timestamp_ms' }),  // ← Manual
});
```

**After (automatic conversion):**

```typescript
export const projects = sqliteTable("projects", {
  id: integer().primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  title: text().notNull(),
  repoUrl: text(),  // ← Automatically becomes "repo_url" in DB
  companyUrl: text(),  // ← Automatically becomes "company_url" in DB

});
```

## What Gets Inferred vs What Doesn't

| Element | Can be inferred? | Example |
|---------|------------------|---------|

## Why?

The table name is the **first argument** to `sqliteTable()` - it's the identity of the table. Drizzle requires it to be explicit:

```typescript

  id: integer().primaryKey(),
  repoUrl: text(),  // ← Column name can be inferred
});
```

```typescript
    index("projects_status_idx").on(table.status),  // Filter by status
]);
```

Good question! Let me explain how this works with your current setup:

---

## Your Current Setup

| File | Contains |
|------|----------|
| `db/schema/better-auth.ts` | Auth tables (users, sessions, accounts, verifications) |
| `db/schema/portfolio.ts` | Portfolio tables (projects, experiences, skills, etc.) |
| `db/migrations/0000_fuzzy_tusk.sql` | Only better-auth tables (already generated) |
| `drizzle.config.ts` | `schema: "./db/schema/*.ts"` → includes BOTH files |

---

## What Will Happen

### If you run `pnpm migrate:generate`:

Drizzle will compare:
- **Current migrations** (0000 = better-auth only)
- **Current schema files** (better-auth + portfolio)

It will generate a **NEW migration file** (e.g., `0001_xxx.sql`) containing **only the portfolio tables** (because better-auth is already in 0000).

### If you run `pnpm migrate:push`:

This **pushes directly to the database** (ignores migration files). On an empty database, it will create **all tables from both schemas**.

---

## Recommended Approach

For a **new empty database**, you have two options:

### Option A: Use Migrations (Recommended for Production)

```bash
# 1. Generate new migration for portfolio tables
pnpm migrate:generate

# 2. Push all migrations to empty database (0000 + 0001)
pnpm migrate:push
```

This creates proper migration history.

### Option B: Use Push Directly (Quick for Development)

```bash
# Just push current schema to database (no new migration file)
pnpm migrate:push
```

This syncs all tables from both schemas directly. No new migration file created.

---

## What Each Script Does

Looking at your `package.json`:

| Script | Command | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `migrate:generate` | `drizzle-kit generate` | Creates migration files from schema changes |
| `migrate:push` | `drizzle-kit push` | Pushes schema directly to DB (skips migration files) |

---

## My Recommendation

Since you have an **empty database** and want proper migration history:

```bash
# 1. Generate migration for portfolio tables
pnpm migrate:generate

# 2. Apply all migrations
pnpm migrate:push
```

After this, your database will have:
- ✅ users, sessions, accounts, verifications (from 0000)
- ✅ projects, experiences, skills, etc. (from 0001)

---

## No New Script Needed

Your current scripts are sufficient! The `schema: "./db/schema/*.ts"` glob pattern already includes both schema files automatically.

Great question! This is a common pattern for admin-only CMS dashboards. Here's how to do it properly:

---

## The Approach

1. **Create a seed script** that runs after migrations
2. **Use environment variables** for admin credentials
3. **Hash the password properly** using Better Auth's internal methods

---

## Step 1: Add Environment Variables

Add these to your `.env` file (and make sure `.env` is in `.gitignore`):

```env
# Admin Credentials (for seeding)
ADMIN_EMAIL=your-email@example.com
ADMIN_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
ADMIN_NAME=Gonzalo
```

## Complete Setup

### 1. Install tsx (for running TypeScript scripts)

```bash
pnpm add -D tsx
```

### 2. Add to your `.env` file

```env
# Admin Credentials (for seeding)
ADMIN_EMAIL=your-email@example.com
ADMIN_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
ADMIN_NAME=Gonzalo
```

### 3. Make sure `.env` is in `.gitignore`

```gitignore
# Environment variables
.env
.env.local
.env*.local
```

---

## New Scripts Added

| Script | Command | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `db:seed` | `pnpm db:seed` | Seeds admin user + site settings |
| `db:setup` | `pnpm db:setup` | Push migrations + seed (all-in-one) |

---

## Usage Flow

For a **new empty database**:

```bash
# Option A: All-in-one
pnpm db:setup

# Option B: Step by step
pnpm migrate:push    # Create tables
pnpm db:seed         # Seed admin user
```

---

## How the Seed Works

1. **Checks if admin exists** - Won't create duplicates
2. **Creates user** in `users` table with `emailVerified: true`
3. **Creates account** in `accounts` table with:
   - `providerId: "credential"` (tells Better Auth it's email/password)
   - `password`: hashed using `scrypt` (same as Better Auth default)
4. **Initializes site settings** if they don't exist

```typescript
async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
    const salt = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
    const derivedKey = (await scryptAsync(password, salt, 64)) as Buffer;
    return `${salt}:${derivedKey.toString("hex")}`;
}
```

### What it does:
1. **Generate a salt** - `randomBytes(16)` creates 16 random bytes, `.toString("hex")` converts to hex string (32 characters)
   - Example salt: `"a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6"`

2. **Hash the password** - `scryptAsync(password, salt, 64)` hashes the password with the salt
   - `64` = output length in bytes (128 hex characters)
   - Returns a Buffer (raw bytes)

3. **Return formatted string** - `salt:hash` format
   - Example: `"a1b2c3...d6:7f8e9d...2a"`

### Why this format?
Better Auth stores passwords as `salt:hash`. When verifying:
1. Split by `:`
2. Use the stored salt to hash the entered password
3. Compare the hashes

What all that call-back based fucntions means ?

_**Agent (model claude-4.5-opus-high-thinking, mode Agent)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The user wants to understand what "callback-based functions" means. This is a fundamental JavaScript/Node.js concept. Let me explain it clearly with examples.</details></think>

---

Great question! Let me explain callbacks in JavaScript/Node.js:

---

## What is a Callback?

A **callback** is a function you pass to another function, which gets called (called back) when the operation is done.

---

## Why Callbacks Exist?

JavaScript is **single-threaded** but needs to handle slow operations (reading files, database queries, network requests) without freezing.

**Solution:** Start the operation, continue with other code, and when it's done, "call back" a function with the result.

---

## Example: Callback Style (Old Way)

```typescript
import { scrypt } from "crypto";

// Callback-based - the OLD way
scrypt("mypassword", "salt", 64, (error, result) => {
    //                           ↑ This function is the "callback"
    //                             It gets called when scrypt finishes
    
    if (error) {
        console.error("Failed:", error);
        return;
    }
    console.log("Hash:", result);
});

console.log("This runs IMMEDIATELY, before scrypt finishes!");
```

**Output order:**
```
This runs IMMEDIATELY, before scrypt finishes!
Hash: <buffer...>   ← This appears later, when scrypt is done
```

---

## The Problem with Callbacks: "Callback Hell"

When you have multiple async operations that depend on each other:

```typescript
// 😱 Callback Hell - nested callbacks
readFile("config.json", (err, config) => {
    if (err) return handleError(err);
    
    connectToDatabase(config, (err, db) => {
        if (err) return handleError(err);
        
        findUser(db, "admin", (err, user) => {
            if (err) return handleError(err);
            
            hashPassword("password", (err, hash) => {
                if (err) return handleError(err);
                
                updateUser(db, user, hash, (err, result) => {
                    if (err) return handleError(err);
                    
                    console.log("Done!", result);
                });
            });
        });
    });
});
```

This is hard to read and maintain!

---

## The Solution: Promises + async/await

### Step 1: Convert Callback to Promise

```typescript
import { promisify } from "util";
import { scrypt } from "crypto";

// Convert callback-based to Promise-based
const scryptAsync = promisify(scrypt);
```

**What `promisify` does:**

| Before (callback) | After (Promise) |
|-------------------|-----------------|
| `scrypt(pw, salt, 64, callback)` | `scryptAsync(pw, salt, 64)` returns a Promise |

---

### Step 2: Use async/await

```typescript
// ✅ Clean and readable with async/await
async function hashPassword(password: string) {
    const salt = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
    const result = await scryptAsync(password, salt, 64);  // ← Waits here
    return `${salt}:${result.toString("hex")}`;
}
```

---

## Visual Comparison

### Callback Style:
```typescript
scrypt("password", "salt", 64, (err, hash) => {
    if (err) throw err;
    console.log(hash);
});
// Code continues immediately, doesn't wait
```

### Promise + async/await Style:
```typescript
const hash = await scryptAsync("password", "salt", 64);
// Code WAITS here until scrypt finishes
console.log(hash);
```

---

## In Your Seed File

```typescript
// Line 6: Import promisify
import { promisify } from "util";

// Line 9: Convert scrypt from callback to Promise
const scryptAsync = promisify(scrypt);

// Line 17: Now we can use await!
const derivedKey = await scryptAsync(password, salt, 64);
```

**Without promisify, you'd have to write:**

```typescript
// 😫 Ugly callback version
function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        const salt = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
        scrypt(password, salt, 64, (err, derivedKey) => {
            if (err) reject(err);
            else resolve(`${salt}:${derivedKey.toString("hex")}`);
        });
    });
}
```

**With promisify:**

```typescript
// ✅ Clean version
async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
    const salt = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
    const derivedKey = await scryptAsync(password, salt, 64);
    return `${salt}:${derivedKey.toString("hex")}`;
}
```

---

## Summary

| Concept | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Callback** | A function passed to another function, called when operation completes |
| **Callback Hell** | Deeply nested callbacks that are hard to read |
| **Promise** | An object representing a future value (pending → resolved/rejected) |
| **async/await** | Syntax sugar to write Promise-based code that looks synchronous |
| **promisify** | Converts callback-based functions to Promise-based |
